namibia: The Namibian dollar (NAD) is pegged 1:1 to the South African Rand. You can use Rand notes everywhere in Namibia, but NAD is not accepted in South Africa.
Etosha's Okaukuejo camp features a floodlit waterhole at night, often drawing rhino and elephant herds just meters from the viewing area.
The Namib Desert is considered the oldest desert in the world, having endured arid or semi-arid conditions for roughly 55 to 80 million years.
When driving on gravel roads, the recommended speed limit is 80 km/h. Most accidents involving tourists happen due to speeding on gravel.
Namibia is one of the few countries in the world to specifically address conservation and protection of natural resources in its constitution.
botswana: The Okavango Delta floods during the dry winter months (June-August), as rainwater from the Angolan highlands takes months to travel down.
Botswana holds the world's largest elephant population, with an estimated 130,000 elephants roaming its parks.
The national currency, Pula, literally translates to 'rain' in Setswana—a reflection of how precious water is in this semi-arid country.
Makgadikgadi Pans is one of the largest salt flats in the world and becomes a breeding ground for thousands of flamingos after good rains.
A 'mokoro' is a traditional dugout canoe used in the Delta. It is propelled by a poler standing at the stern, similar to punting.
south-africa: South Africa has three capital cities: Pretoria (executive), Cape Town (legislative), and Bloemfontein (judicial).
Table Mountain in Cape Town hosts over 1,500 species of plants, more plant species than the entire United Kingdom.
Kruger National Park is roughly the same size as Israel or the US state of New Jersey.
South Africa is the only country in the entire world that has voluntarily dismantled its nuclear weapons program.
The country has 12 official languages, with Zulu, Xhosa, Afrikaans, and English being the most widely spoken.
zambia: Victoria Falls is locally known as 'Mosi-oa-Tunya', which translates to 'The Smoke That Thunders'.
Zambia relies heavily on hydropower, with the Kariba Dam supplying much of the country's electricity.
The South Luangwa National Park is famous as the birthplace of the 'walking safari'.
During the dry season, you can swim in the Devil's Pool—a natural infinity pool right on the edge of Victoria Falls.
Every year, millions of straw-colored fruit bats migrate to Kasanka National Park, creating one of the largest mammal migrations on Earth.
zimbabwe: Zimbabwe has the highest literacy rate in Africa, hovering around 90%.
The country is home to the Great Zimbabwe ruins, the largest ancient structure south of the Sahara.
Due to historic hyperinflation, Zimbabwe operates a multi-currency system. The US Dollar is widely accepted and preferred.
Hwange National Park is the largest park in Zimbabwe and is particularly famous for its large herds of elephants and Cape wild dogs.
Lake Kariba is the world's largest man-made lake and reservoir by volume.
malawi: Lake Malawi contains more species of fish than any other lake in the world, many of which are endemic cichlids.
Malawi is often called the 'Warm Heart of Africa' due to the legendary friendliness and hospitality of its people.
Lake Malawi takes up about one-third of the country's total area.
Mount Mulanje, rising to 3,002 meters, is the highest peak in south-central Africa.
Chambo, a type of tilapia found in Lake Malawi, is considered a national delicacy.
mozambique: Mozambique has a coastline stretching over 2,500 kilometers along the Indian Ocean.
The official language is Portuguese, reflecting its history as a Portuguese colony until 1975.
Gorongosa National Park is undergoing one of the most successful wildlife restoration projects in the world after being decimated by civil war.
The Quirimbas Archipelago consists of over 30 coral islands and is renowned for its pristine marine life.
Piri-piri (a spicy chili sauce) is a staple in Mozambican cuisine, heavily influencing dishes like peri-peri chicken.
lesotho: Lesotho is the only independent state in the world that lies entirely above 1,000 meters in elevation.
It is completely surrounded by South Africa, making it one of only three enclaved countries in the world.
The traditional Basotho blanket is a common sight and serves as a status symbol and cultural identifier.
Afriski, situated in the Maluti Mountains, is one of the few ski resorts in Africa.
The country is known as the 'Kingdom in the Sky' due to its high altitude.
eswatini: Eswatini (formerly Swaziland) is one of the few remaining absolute monarchies in the world.
The Umhlanga, or Reed Dance, is an annual cultural event where thousands of Swazi maidens gather to perform for the Queen Mother.
Hlane Royal National Park is home to the largest herds of game in the country and is a great place to see rhinos.
The country changed its name from Swaziland to Eswatini in 2018 to mark 50 years of independence.
Despite its small size, Eswatini has a diverse landscape ranging from mountains to savannas.
